# **Cohocton and Dutch Hill Wind Farms Year 2 Post-Construction Monitoring Report, 2010**

for the Cohocton and Dutch Hill Wind Farms in Cohocton, New York

## Prepared for

Canandaigua Power Partners, LLC and Canandaigua Power Partners II, LLC One Dana Street, Second Floor Portland, ME  04101

## Prepared by

Stantec Consulting Services Inc. 30 Park Drive Topsham, ME  04086

January 2011

## **Executive Summary**

The Cohocton and Dutch Hill Wind Farms (Project) consist of 35 and 15 Clipper Liberty 2.5 MW turbines, respectively.  The Project is located in Steuben County, New York and is situated in agricultural and forested uplands.  Both facilities became fully operational as of January 2009. The turbines at Cohocton and Dutch Hill have a maximum height of 131 meters (m; 429 feet [’]) (tower and blade-tip height combined).  Twenty-three turbines at Cohocton and seven turbines at Dutch Hill are lit with FAA approved lighting.  For the purposes of this report, the following Project area locations are considered one Project: Cohocton (Pine Hill, Lent Hill, and Brown Hill) and Dutch Hill.

As part of the permit conditions for the Project, a second year of post-construction monitoring was conducted during Year 2 of operation by Stantec Consulting Services Inc. (Stantec) on behalf of Canandaigua Power Partners, LLC (CPP) and Canandaigua Power Partners II, LLC (CPP II), subsidiaries of First Wind Management, LLC (First Wind).  Year 2 of survey followed a first year of effort in 2009 during which Stantec evaluated bird and bat fatality, breeding bird and acoustic bat activity, as well as vegetation conditions in relation to search techniques and analytical methodologies.  The methodologies for the second year of study were based on the findings and results of the 2009 study.   This second year of post-construction monitoring involved a bird and bat mortality study and bat acoustic monitoring.  The objectives of postconstruction monitoring were to:

- 1) estimate bird and bat fatality rates and to determine if mortality represents an ecologically significant impact;

- 2) determine if there are significant differences in mortality at turbines with different project design or landscape features; and to

- 3) determine the activity of bats, relative to mortality and weather, in the proximity of operating turbines..

The 2010 Project work plan was developed by First Wind in cooperation with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) and US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS).  The work plan is based on communication with NYSDEC, USFWS, the _Guidelines for Conducting Bird and Bat Studies at Commercial Wind Energy Projects_ (NYSDEC 2009) and the _Interim Guidelines to Avoid and Minimize Wildlife Impacts from Wind Turbines_ (USFWS 2003).  The 2010 study protocol incorporated the findings of the first year of monitoring at the Project and was modified from the 2009 study protocol during communications with NYDEC and USFWS.

## _Bird and Bat Mortality Survey_

Bird and bat mortality searches were scheduled at the Project for 26 consecutive weeks between April 26 and October 22, 2010.  A total of 17 turbines were included in standardized mortality searches (34% of 50 total turbines at Cohocton and Dutch Hill combined).  Weekly searches were conducted at search turbines, except from July 15 to September 17 when daily searches were conducted at five turbines.  Weekly searches continued at the other 12 turbines during this period.

The standard search area at turbine plots was 120 m by 120 m (393’ by 393’), except at those plots abutting woodlots or agricultural crops such as corn or soy where searches were conducted out to the forest or agricultural field edge.  All search turbines underwent vegetation management (mowing or harvesting) as needed over the course of the study period. Out of 387 scheduled weekly turbine searches, a total of 365 (94%) were conducted.  Out of 325 scheduled daily turbine searches, a total of 299 (92%) were conducted.  Occasionally, scheduled turbine searches could not be completed due to maintenance activities or weather conditions.

A total of 63 bats were found during the 2010 mortality searches: 32 were found at daily searched turbines, 26 were found at weekly searched turbines, and 5 were found incidentally. Species included hoary bat ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ) (24), eastern red bat ( _Lasiurus borealis_ ) (13), little brown bat ( _Myotis lucifugus_ ) (11), silver-haired bat ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ ) (9), big brown bat ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ ) (4), northern long-eared bat ( _Myotis septentrionalis_ ) (1), and unidentified bat (1).  This compares to 69 total bats found during the 2009 survey effort.

A total of nine bird fatalities were found: four were found at daily searched turbines, four were found at weekly searched turbines, and one was found incidentally.  Species found as fatalities include: common yellowthroat ( _Geothlypis trichas_ ) (2), magnolia warbler ( _Dendroica magnolia_ ) (2), red-eyed vireo ( _Vireo olivaceus_ ) (1), red-tailed hawk ( _Buteo jamaicensis_ ) (1), and unidentified passerine (3).  A total of 18 bird fatalities were documented in 2009.

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted to determine the percent of carcasses that were recovered by searchers.  Overall searcher efficiency in 2010 was 46 percent for bats and 60 percent for birds.  In 2009, searcher efficiency was 24 percent for bats and 38 percent for birds.

Carcass removal trials were conducted to determine what percent of carcasses were not removed by scavengers in search plots, and thus were available for detection.  Carcass removal trials indicated that on Day 1 (for the daily search interval) 73 percent of bat carcasses remained, and 81 percent of bird carcasses remained; on Day 4 (for the weekly search interval), 33 percent of bat carcasses remained, and 48 percent of bird carcasses remained.   This compared to 93 percent of bat carcasses and 89 percent of bird carcasses remaining on Day 1; and 63 percent of bat carcasses and 69 percent of bird carcasses remaining on Day 4 in 2009.

The average distance bat carcasses were found from the turbines was 27.05 m (88.7’).  Bat carcass distances ranged from 0.45 m to 63 m (1.46’ to 206.6’).  The average distance bird carcasses were found from the turbines was 35.1 m (115’).  Bird carcass distances from turbines ranged from 18 to 56 m (59’ to 183.6’).

The statistical analysis for the distribution of carcasses found during the 2010 surveys indicated an equal distribution of carcasses among turbines included in weekly mortality searches. Consistent with the 2009 results, bat mortality was significantly higher at fields adjacent to forest sites than at field sites.  Also consistent with the previous year, there were no relationships between carcass locations and turbines with and without FAA lighting.  Like 2009, there was no significant difference between carcass locations among turbines located at the middle or end of turbine strings, and there was no relationship between carcasses and turbines located at edge or non-edge locations of plateaus in 2010.  Analysis of the 2010 data indicated

differences in the numbers of fatalities at turbines within different Project area locations: there was a significant difference between bird mortality at Lent Hill and Brown Hill; a significant difference between bat mortality at Lent Hill, Brown Hill, and Dutch Hill; and a significant difference between bat mortality at Lent Hill and Brown Hill.

In 2010, estimates of bat fatality rates ranged from 5.04 to 25.62 bats per turbine per study period (bats/turbine/study period) or 3.36 to 17.08 bats per megawatt per study period ([bats/MW/study period]).  The 2010 estimates of bat mortality at Cohocton and Dutch Hill, based on weekly searches, were within the range of mortality detected at wind farms in New York.  When interpreting results, it should be considered that the 2010 mortality estimate based on daily searches is representative of the peak bat fatality period from mid-July to midSeptember only.  Therefore, the daily mortality estimate is not indicative of the full study period. Consequently, this estimate is not directly comparable to other sites where daily surveys were conducted for the full study period (spring through fall).  Estimates of bird fatality rates ranged from 0.82 to 2.06 birds/turbine/study period (0.55 to1.37 birds/MW/study period).  The 2010 fatality estimates for birds and bats were lower than the 2009 estimates.  Additionally, the confidence intervals for the estimates of total fatalities are narrower in 2010 than in 2009, meaning there is a higher confidence in the 2010 estimates.  The 2010 estimates of bird and bat fatality are within the range of mortality documented at other recent studies in the region.

## _Bat Detector Survey_

During the 2010 post-construction monitoring study, three SD1 Anabat detectors (Titley Electronics Pty Ltd.) were deployed at varying heights in three locations in the Project area. The intent of the acoustic bat surveys was to document bat activity patterns and general species composition from April through October and document bat activity patterns in relation to the mortality survey data.  Two detectors were positioned in trees adjacent to mortality search turbines at 2 and 2.5 m elevations.  A third detector was deployed in a met tower approximately 40 m above the ground.  The three detectors combined were operable for a total of 434 detector nights, at all detectors combined.  Occasional equipment malfunctions occurred resulting in a 78 percent operation success.

Detectors operated from April 21 through October 23, 2010 and recorded a total of 46,293 bat call sequences over a period of 434 detector nights, resulting in an overall detection rate of 106.7 bat call sequences per detector night.  Nightly bat activity was variable at all detectors, but monthly detection rates generally increased through June and July, then decreased through the end of the survey at all detectors.  The turbine 2A tree detector recorded the most calls and had the highest overall detection rate (309.0 call sequences per detector night).   However, there were no bat fatalities documented at this turbine.

More than half (59%) of all recorded call sequences belonged to the _Myotis_ guild, and together with the high frequency unknown guild, comprised approximately 69 percent of all recorded sequences.  Approximately 24 percent of call sequences were assigned to the big brown/silverhaired guild, four percent to the low-frequency unknown guild, two percent to the hoary bat guild, and one percent to the eastern red bat/tri-colored guild.

## **1.0 Introduction**

The Cohocton and Dutch Hill Wind Farms (Project) consist of 35 and 15 Clipper Liberty 2.5 MW turbines, respectively.  Although the two facilities were permitted separately and considered individual projects, for the purposes of this study, the two projects are considered one based on the close proximity of the sites and their similar landscape settings.  The Project is located in Steuben County, New York and is situated in agricultural and forested uplands.  The Project became fully operational as of January 2009.  The Cohocton and Dutch Hill turbines have a maximum height of 131 meters (m; 429 feet [’]) (tower and blade-tip height combined).  Twentythree turbines at Cohocton and seven at Dutch Hill are lit with FAA approved lighting (Figure 1- 1).

As part of the permit conditions for the Project, a second year of post-construction monitoring was conducted during Year 2 of operation by Stantec Consulting Services Inc. (Stantec) on behalf of Canandaigua Power Partners, LLC (CPP) and Canandaigua Power Partners II, LLC (CPP II), subsidiaries of First Wind Management, LLC (First Wind).  This second year of postconstruction monitoring involved a bird and bat mortality study and bat acoustic monitoring.  The objectives of post-construction monitoring were to:

- 1) estimate bird and bat fatality rates and to determine if mortality represents an ecologically significant impact;

- 2) determine if there are significant differences in mortality at turbines with different project design or landscape features; and to

- 3) determine the activity of bats, relative to mortality and weather, in the proximity of operating turbines..

The 2010 Project work plan was developed by First Wind in cooperation with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) and US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS).  The work plan is based on communication with NYSDEC, USFWS, the _Guidelines for Conducting Bird and Bat Studies at Commercial Wind Energy Projects_ (NYSDEC 2009) and the _Interim Guidelines to Avoid and Minimize Wildlife Impacts from Wind Turbines_ (USFWS 2003).  The 2010 study protocol also incorporated the findings of the first year of monitoring at the Project.  The 2009 pilot study investigated the effects of mowing on searcher efficiency and determined that mowing search plots increased the accuracy of estimates of bird and bat mortality rates (Stantec 2010b).  Therefore, during the 2010 study, First Wind mowed all search plots on a regular basis where possible.  The timing of the initiation and completion of fatality searches was planned around the peak periods of fatalities found in the spring and fall in 2009. In 2010, the search plot size was reduced 10 m by 10 m (33’ by 33’) to focus effort on areas where the majority of carcasses were found during the 2009 searches.  Finally, instead of searching a daily sub-set of turbines throughout the study period, search effort was increased from weekly to daily at a sub-set of turbines during the peak period of bat mortality and acoustic activity documented in 2009 (mid-July to mid-September).

## **1.1 PROJECT AREA DESCRIPTION**

The Cohocton and Dutch Hill Wind Farms are located in the Town of Cohocton, Steuben County, New York.  The Project occurs within the Central Appalachians and Finger Lakes Highlands sub-zones of the Appalachian Plateau Eco-zone of New York (Dickinson 1983 and Will _et al_ . 1982 as cited in Andrle and Caroll 1988).  The topography of this region in southwestern New York consists of long valleys and rolling ridges, roughly orientated in a north to south direction.  The Appalachian Plateau consists of highlands that are rather flat-topped with deeply dissected valleys.  Typical weather conditions include cold, snowy winters and cool, wet summers.  Northern hardwoods are the dominant forest canopy species in the region, although south-facing slopes are often dominated by oaks and other hardwood species typically found in central Appalachia.  Pine and hemlock are also common species.  Agricultural land uses dominate the landscape with forests or scattered woodlands occupying approximately onethird of the Eco-zone.  In general, forested habitats are found on the steep side-slopes of plateaus and within the narrow stream valleys.  Open agricultural habitats are most common in wide river valley bottoms and on the tops of plateaus.

The Finger Lakes Highlands and Central Appalachians sub-zones share similar characteristics with the Appalachian Plateau eco-zone.  Elevations are generally higher in the Central Appalachians (average elevation of 457 m to 700 m; 1,500’ to 2,300’) than in the Finger Lakes Highlands (average elevation of 305 m to 518 m; 1,000’ to 1,700’).

The Cohocton and Dutch Hill Wind Farms are located on plateaus that are oriented northeast to southwest. The general elevations of the Project range from 600 m to 655 m (1,968’ to 2,150’). Narrow, steep-sided stream valleys dissect the plateaus from all directions and are forested with hemlock and a mixture of hardwoods.  The Cohocton River Valley lies to the west and south of the Project and the Twelve-mile Stream Valley lies to the east.  The Naples Creek Valley lies to the north and drains into the nearby Canandaigua Lake.  Included in this watershed is the 6,100-acre High Tor Wildlife Management Area, which includes a diversity of upland and wetland habitats at the southern end of Canandaigua Lake.

The predominant land use in the area is agricultural, with open fields comprising more than twothirds of each site.  Forested habitats include oaks, northern hardwoods, pine, and hemlock. Mature forest stands are common, as are areas of young, secondary growth, including hedgerows, wood borders, and old fields.  The turbines are located primarily in active agricultural fields adjacent to woodlots.  Individual landowner management practices have continued in the areas directly adjacent to turbines.  Specific cover crops in the fields adjacent to turbines vary by landowner, and vary further on a year-to-year basis.  Crops primarily include hay, alfalfa, soy, and corn.  Areas directly around the turbine bases had been seeded and mulched after construction and after maintenance activities in 2009.  In 2010, grass and clover grew thickly in those areas.   The turbine driveways leading up to the turbine pads consist of gravel and crushed stone.

The two facilities were permitted separately and are considered individual Projects.  However, for the purposes of this study, the two Projects (Cohocton: Lent Hill, Pine Hill, and Brown Hill; and Dutch Hill) are considered one based on their close proximity to each other and their similar landscape settings.  Therefore, the term “Project” refers to both wind farms and the facilities are only discussed separately for discussion of the analyses run to compare results at distinct locations within the Project.

## **2.0 Bird and Bat Mortality Survey**

## **2.1 METHODS**

## **2.1.1 Standardized Bird and Bat Mortality Searches**

Bird and bat mortality searches were scheduled to occur at the Cohocton and Dutch Hill Wind Farms for 26 consecutive weeks between April 26 and October 22, 2010.  This timeframe covered four distinct seasons:

- spring migration (April 26 to May 31);

- summer – bird nesting and bat pup-rearing period (June 1 to July 14);

- late-summer – bat activity period (July 15 to August 15); and

- fall migration (August 16 to October 22).

A total of 17 turbines were included in standardized mortality searches (34% of 50 total turbines at Cohocton and Dutch Hill combined) (Figure 2-1).  Weekly mortality surveys were conducted at all 17 search turbines, except from July 15 to September 17 when daily searches were conducted at five turbines and weekly searches continued at the other 12 turbines.  All search turbines underwent vegetation management as needed over the course of the study period. Search turbines were chosen based on habitat, location in Project area, as well as expected level of landowner cooperation.

The standard search area at turbine plots was 120 m by 120 m (393’ by 393’) except at those plots abutting woodlots or agricultural crops (such as corn or soy) where searches were conducted out to the forest or agricultural field edge.  Garmin eTREX GPS units were used to indicate the start and end points of transects at plots where the searchable area was reduced. Searches were mainly conducted in hay, grass, alfalfa, and wheat fields.  At plots where the full area could be searched, 24 north-to-south[2] oriented transects were established 5 m (16.4’) apart.  The ends of transects were marked with flagged wooden stakes or flagged trees when permissible by the landowner.

A Stantec biologist thoroughly trained in the study protocols conducted the weekly turbine searches.  The process required two biologists to complete all searches during the latesummer/early fall period when daily surveys were also conducted at five turbines.  During searches, the biologist(s) would walk at a rate of approximately 45 to 60 m (148’ to197’) per minute, searching on both sides of transects for bird or bat fatalities.  Any fatality found along or between transects was documented.  All intact bird or bat carcasses or remnants of scavenged carcasses (a cluster of feathers representing more than a molt, or a patch of skin and bone) were documented as fatalities.

> 2 Transects were oriented north-to-south with the exception of transects in the plots of turbines 2A and 1A where the landowner requested that the transect stakes be parallel to rows that he used for mowing.

For each fatality found, the following information was recorded on standardized datasheets:

- date;

- surveyor;

- time discovered;

- turbine number;

- carcass distance from turbine (determined with a laser range finder);

- carcass direction from turbine (compass reading);

- carcass distance and direction from observer when found;

- ground conditions (vegetation type and height, wet, dry, etc.);

- species identification (including age, sex, and reproductive condition when possible),

- • carcass position;

- stage of decomposition of the carcass (previous night, 2 to 3 days, 4 to 7 days, 7 to 14 days, greater than 2 weeks);

- evidence of scavenger activity; and

- additional notes when necessary.

All carcasses were collected and frozen.  Some of the carcasses that were of fresh disposition (believed to have collided the night before) were later used for carcass removal trials.

Ground conditions including cover type, relative size of area of cover type (subject to change due to plowing and harvesting), and vegetation height were documented weekly at each search turbine.  When vegetation height grew over six inches (“), First Wind was notified that mowing was needed.

## **2.1.2 Weather Data**

On nights prior to mortality searches, sky conditions - including cloud height, cloud type, and percent cloud cover - were recorded from the field house in Bristol, NY.  Additional weather and operational information – wind speed, hub speed, wind direction, air temperature, and barometric pressure – were collected from a turbine nacelle (turbine 2A on Dutch Hill) and/or from the met tower on Pine Hill.

## **2.1.3 Incidental Mortality Findings and Wildlife Observations**

Any fatalities found by maintenance personnel or by surveyors outside of the standardized searches were documented (including all information collected for carcasses found during standard searches) and removed from the study area.  These findings were reported as incidental and were not included in the estimates of total mortality for birds and bats. However, incidental findings were included in the spatial and temporal summaries of fatalities.

While surveyors were on-site for mortality searches, incidental wildlife-turbine interaction observations were documented on standardized datasheets (including date, location, whether it was a species of conservation concern, any turbine-interaction behaviors, distance from nearest turbine, etc).  The date, species, location, proximity to Project structures, and description of the animal’s general activity - particularly any interactions with turbines – were recorded.

## **2.1.4 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

The objective of searcher efficiency trials was to estimate the percent of bird and bat carcasses that may go undetected during standardized searches.  It was the goal to conduct multiple searcher efficiency trials over the course of the survey period.  The study targeted the use of at least 10 carcasses per trial, using native bird and bat species.  The trials used small and medium-to-large bird carcasses, and small and medium-to-large bat carcasses.  Carcasses found during mortality searches, as well as additional carcasses provided by a wildlife rehabilitation center, were used during the trials.

Early in the morning of the trials and prior to the arrival of searchers, a biologist (trial coordinator) placed carcasses at turbines scheduled to be searched that day.  Trial coordinators took care to be discreet when setting up trials so that surveyors being tested would be unaware. Carcasses were placed in search plots within a variety of ground cover types (bare ground, corn, hayfield, soybean, etc.).  Carcasses were discreetly marked with string or an elastic band so that, when found, the surveyor would be able to distinguish trial carcasses from actual fatalities.  Trial carcasses recovered by the surveyor were collected.  After the test, the trial coordinator tallied those trial carcasses that were found to determine the number of carcasses recovered by the surveyor.

## **2.1.5 Carcass Removal Rate Trials**

Carcass removal trials were conducted to determine the percent of carcasses removed by scavengers between search intervals.  It was the objective to conduct multiple trials over the course of the study period.  Individual trials targeted the use of 10 carcasses in good disposition (fresh but previously frozen), using native bird and bat species.  As with the searcher efficiency trials, the carcass removal trials used small and medium-to-large bird carcasses, and small and medium-to-large bats.  Carcasses found during mortality searches, as well as additional carcasses provided by a wildlife rehabilitation center, were used in trials, and were marked with string or an elastic band to distinguish trial birds and bats from actual fatalities.  During trials, carcasses were placed at turbines throughout the Project area, and within a variety of ground cover types.

The status of the carcasses was monitored daily over a period of 28 days.  All evidence of insect, mammalian, or avian scavenging was noted on standardized datasheets.  A carcass was considered present if it was partially scavenged but still readily detectable to a surveyor.  A carcass was considered absent if it was completely removed or only a few feathers or other remains were left so that it was not readily detectable.  All remaining carcasses were removed from search plots on day 28.

## **2.1.6 Vegetation Management**

All search plots underwent vegetation management including mowing by First Wind and mowing/harvesting by landowners.  Vegetation management was conducted as needed throughout the study period.

## **2.1.7 ANHM Bat Genetic Isotope and White-nose Syndrome Project**

CPP, CPP II, and Stantec are participating in the American Natural History Museum (ANHM) bat genetic isotope and white-nose syndrome project by donating bat carcasses found at Cohocton and Dutch Hill during the 2010 mortality searches.  All bat carcasses not previously

used for scavenger carcass removal trials will be submitted to ANHM, pending acceptance by the ANHM.

## **2.1.8 Data Summaries and Statistical Analysis**

Stantec summarized the seasonal timing of fatalities, the timing of fatality events, weather conditions, and the locations carcasses were found in relation to the turbines. These analyses included all carcasses found during the study period (including those carcasses found daily, weekly, and incidentally).  It is important to note survey effort varied among all turbines when interpreting the results (daily searches versus weekly searches versus incidental findings).

The statistical analysis of the spatial and temporal distribution of fatalities, as well as the estimate of fatality rates for birds and bats, considered only those carcasses found during standard searches (i.e., not those carcasses found incidentally), and the analysis was separate for fatalities found at daily versus weekly searched turbines.  The following lists of attributes were included in the data analysis:

1. Seasonal timing of all fatalities (daily, weekly, and incidentals).

- The numbers of bird and bat fatalities were summarized by season.

2. Fatality events and weather condition comparisons (daily, weekly and incidentals).

- For those birds and bats found in a fresh disposition (date of collision was believed to be the previous night), weather conditions were summarized for the nights of collision.

3. Spatial distribution of all fatalities (daily, weekly and incidentals).

- The range of distances for birds and bats from the towers and the average distance of bird and bat fatalities from towers were summarized.

4. Spatial distribution of fatalities found during standard searches (daily and weekly)

- the evenness of distribution of fatalities at individual turbines;

- the location of fatalities at turbines in different landscapes settings (field, or field directly adjacent to forest);

- the location of fatalities at FAA lit verses unlit turbines;

- the location of fatalities at turbines within different Project locations (Lent Hill/Pine Hill, Dutch Hill, or Brown Hill);

- the location of fatalities at turbines positioned at the end or middle of turbine strings (mid-strings were considered those bordered by surrounding turbines, while end-strings included those at the end or edge of turbine rows); and

- the location of fatalities at turbines at the edge or non-edge of a plateau.

The statistical analysis software program SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC) was used to compare bird and bat fatalities with different landscape and turbine design characteristics. Count data (i.e., number of birds or bats found at turbines) is inherently non-normal distribution data; therefore, it is correctly modeled as Poisson distribution - a probability distribution which occurs when counting the number of occurrences of a rare event in a long series of trials. Accordingly, nonparametric (distribution free) statistical tests were used.  Chi-square tests for

goodness-of-fit were run to determine if bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were evenly distributed among turbines.  This analysis was run for search turbines that had fatalities, then with search turbines both with-and-without fatalities.  Bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were compared among turbines in two different landscape settings (field, or field directly adjacent to forest) using Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests.  Bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were compared among turbines located in three different Project locations (Lent Hill/Pine Hill, Dutch Hill, or Brown Hill) using Kruskal-Wallis tests.  Bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were compared among turbines located in two different positions, mid-string or end-string, using Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests.  Bird, bat, and all fatalities combined were compared between FAA lit and unlit turbines using Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests.  Finally, Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests were used to compare bird, bat, and all fatalities combined at turbines located on the edge or non-edge of plateaus.  A probability value for the significance level of 0.05 was chosen prior to analysis.

## _Estimate of Fatality Rates_

The results of the separate searcher efficiency trails were pooled for bird and bat carcasses. The searcher efficiency rate was determined as the total number of carcasses found divided by the total number of carcasses placed.

The results of the carcass removal trials were also pooled for bird and bat carcasses.  The period between carcass fall and discovery is approximately half the actual search interval, rounded up by to a whole day (i.e., for a weekly search interval, this value is 3.5 days; therefore, this period is rounded up to 4 days) (Jain _et al_ . 2007, 2008, 2009a).  For a daily search interval, this period is one day.  Therefore, the analysis factored the percent of trial carcasses that remained visible on Day 1 for daily searches and Day 4 for weekly searches.

A correction factor was applied to the raw number of carcasses found at individual turbines to account for the areas that were not searchable within the 120 m by 120 m (14,400 square meters [sq. m]) search plots.  Plots in every cover type were searched except the forested areas.  Methods were modified from those presented by Fielder _et al._ 2007 and Jain _et al._ 2009d.  For those plots where the full area could not be searched, the boundary of the searchable area was determined using Garmin eTREX GPS plot boundary points and the percentage of the searchable area within these reduced search plots then calculated.  The number of bird and bat fatalities found at each turbine with a reduced search area was divided by the percent area searched within each of the reduced plots in order to calculate a corrected number of fatalities at those individual turbines.

The estimates of the rates of bird and bat mortality (fatalities per turbine per study period, fatalities per megawatt per study period, and fatalities per rotor-swept area per study period) for the Project were modeled after methods described by Jain _et al._ (2007, 2008, 2009a).  The total estimate of mortality per study period (ĉ) was based on the total number of birds and bats found, adjusted for searchable area (C), the proportion of turbines searched (Ps), the percent of carcasses found by the surveyor (Se), and the percent of carcasses not removed by scavengers (Sc).  Estimates were calculated for daily and weekly turbine searches.

The variances for the mortality estimates were calculated as described by Jain et al. (2007, 2008, 2009a).

The standard deviation was then calculated based on the square root of the variance divided by the square root of the number of searched turbines for each search interval, multiplied by a factor of 95 percent confidence (1.96) to determine confidence intervals for each estimate.  For statistical analyses in general, a confidence interval, or range of possible values, is calculated when there is uncertainty in the number of individuals or population in a dataset.

## **2.2.2 Bird and Bat Fatalities**

## **2.2.5 Spatial Distribution of Fatalities**

Bat fatalities were found at 13 of 17 weekly searched turbines and at five of five daily searched turbines.  The number of bat fatalities at individual weekly searched turbines ranged from one to four bats and one to 14 bats at individual daily searched turbines.

Bird fatalities were found at 4 different turbines out of the 17 weekly searched turbines and four of five daily searched turbines.  At turbines where bird fatalities were found during weekly or daily searched turbines only one fatality was found.

The results of the statistical analysis for the spatial distribution of carcasses are summarized below.  Since only five turbines were searched daily, comparisons between groups (i.e., lit verses unlit turbines) have very small sample sizes.  Consequently, the statistical tests have little to no power to identify significant differences between groups even if differences exist.  All the same tests ran for weekly searched turbines were also run for daily searched turbines, and all test results were not significant.  The results of daily searched turbine comparisons are not included here due to the lack of statistical power from the small sample sizes.

- the evenness of distribution of fatalities at individual turbines included in weekly searched turbines

Chi-square (χ-square) tests for goodness-of-fit showed that bird fatalities were evenly distributed among turbines with and without fatalities (χ-square = 13.00, degrees of freedom - [d.f.]= 16).  Bat fatalities were evenly distributed among turbines with and without fatalities (χ square = 15.85, d.f. = 16).  Combined bird and bat fatalities were evenly distributed among turbines with and without fatalities (χ-square = 14.20, d.f. = 16).

Bird fatalities were evenly distributed among turbines with fatalities (χ-square = 0, d.f. = 3).  Bat fatalities were evenly distributed among turbines with fatalities (χ-square = 6, d.f. = 12). Combined bird and bat fatalities were evenly distributed among turbines with fatalities (χ-square = 6.4, d.f. = 13).

- the location of fatalities at turbines in different landscapes settings (field, or field directly adjacent to forest) at weekly searched turbines

The Wilcoxon Rank Sum Tests determined that there is no significant difference between bird mortality and the two landscape features (W = 73, probability < 0.05 [p] = 0.9479).  Bat mortality was significantly higher at field adjacent to forest sites than at field sites (W = 51.5, p = 0.0479). There was no significant difference between combined bird and bat mortality and the two landscape features (W = 52, p = 0.0526).

- the location of fatalities at FAA lit verses unlit weekly searched turbines

## **2.3 DISCUSSION**

The statistical analysis for the distribution of carcasses found during the 2010 surveys indicated an equal distribution of carcasses among turbines included in weekly mortality searches.  This indicates that there was no individual turbine which contributed a substantially higher number of bird or bat fatalities.  However, one daily searched turbine, turbine 25, had a relatively high number of bat fatalities (n=14), particularly after the number of bat carcasses found was corrected for non-searchable area (n=25).  Consistent with the 2009 results, bat mortality was significantly higher at fields located adjacent to forest sites than at distinct field sites.  Also consistent with the previous year, there were no relationships between carcass locations and turbines with and without FAA lighting.  Also consistent with the previous year, there was no significant difference between carcass locations among turbines located at the middle or end of turbine strings, and there was no relationship between carcasses and turbines located at edge or non-edge plateau locations.  Analysis of the 2010 data indicated a significant difference between bird mortality at Lent Hill and Brown Hill; a significant difference between bat mortality at Lent Hill, Brown Hill, and Dutch Hill; and a significant difference between bat mortality at Lent Hill and Brown Hill.  The factors influencing significant differences in bird and bat fatality among the three Project area locations are beyond the scope of this study.  However, as there was a significant relationship between bat fatalities and landscape setting, it may be that landscape and habitat features influence the activity of bats, and likely birds as well, in different Project area locations.

Search plots were mowed throughout the 2010 study period.  As a result, searcher efficiency for the 2010 study was higher than during the 2009 study when only a subset of turbines underwent vegetation management and the other search turbines experienced normal land use practices. Overall searcher efficiency for bats and birds in 2010 was 46 and 60 percent, respectively; compared to 24 and 38 percent for bats and birds, respectively, in 2009.  As a result, the confidence intervals for the estimates of total fatalities are narrower in 2010 than in 2009, meaning there is a higher confidence in the 2010 estimates. In general, estimates of bat mortality have been found to be highest in the eastern U.S., particularly along forested ridgelines (Arnett _et al._ 2008).  Emerging bat fatality data suggests that latitude, or geographic location, may influence bat mortality at wind farms as notably higher estimates of bat kills per turbine per study period have been documented in the southeastern U.S. (Arnett 2005, Fielder _et al._ 2007, Arnett _et al._ 2008), and lower in other regions such as the Rocky Mountains or the Pacific Northwest (Arnett _et al._ 2008).  However, regional differences in bat habitat and populations limit the value of direct comparison among these regions. Therefore, this report considers other studies from the east and midwest because their geographic location, species present, and the regional populations of these species, are most applicable to the Project.  Bat mortality in the region has ranged from 0.17 bats/turbine/study period (Mars Hill, Maine 2008) to 63.9 bats/turbine/study period (Buffalo Mountain, Tennessee 2005) (Table 2-12).

The 2010 estimates of bat mortality at Cohocton and Dutch Hill, based on weekly searches, were within the range of mortality detected at wind farms in New York (Table 2-12).  The 2010 bat mortality estimate based on daily searches at Cohocton and Dutch Hill was relatively high for most existing sites in New York, but similar to the estimate of bat fatality at Maple Ridge based on daily searches in 2006 (20.31 bats/turbine/study period) (Table 2-12; Jain _et al._ 2007). However, when interpreting these results it should be considered that the Cohocton and Dutch Hill 2010 mortality estimate based on daily searches is representative of the peak bat fatality period from mid-July to mid-September only.  This is the timeframe that daily searches at Cohocton and Dutch Hill were conducted.  Therefore, the daily mortality estimate is not indicative of the full study period.  Consequently, this estimate is not directly comparable to other sites where daily surveys were conducted for the full study period (spring through fall).

The highest estimates of bat fatality at Cohocton and Dutch Hill in 2009 and 2010 were based on daily searches, and the confidence intervals for these estimates were the widest ranging (i.e. least amount of confidence in daily estimates).  The wider ranging confidence intervals are influenced by the smaller sample sizes of daily searched turbines in 2009 and 2010.  The 2010 estimates of bat mortality were nearly half of what they were in 2009.  Again, the confidence

intervals for the estimates of total bat fatalities are narrower in 2010 than in 2009, meaning there is a higher confidence in the 2010 estimates.

There were six different species of bat (not including one unidentified species) found as fatalities during the 2010 study; none of these species are listed in the state of New York.  Hoary bat and eastern red bat represented the majority of bat species found.  These results are consistent with other studies, as the majority of individuals of bats species at wind farms in the east mainly consist of the long-distance migratory species such as hoary bat, silver-haired bat, and eastern red bat (Arnett _et al._ 2008).  During the 2010 study at Cohocton and Dutch Hill, the majority of bats were found during the summer bat pup-rearing period and during the late-summer bat activity period.  The majority of bat fatalities at wind farms around the world involve migratory bats during fall migration (Arnett _et al_ . 2008, Baerwald and Barclay 2009).

Estimates of avian fatalities reported for studies conducted in the east and upper midwest, have ranged from 0.33 birds/turbine/study period (Buffalo Ridge, Minnesota 1995) to 9.48 birds/turbine/study period (Maple Ridge, New York 2006) (Table 2-12). The results of the Cohocton and Dutch Hill mortality study are consistent with the findings of other studies in the region in terms of species involved in collisions, seasonal timing of the majority of collisions, and the number of individuals involved in collisions (NRC 2007, Table 2-12).  Studies suggest that nocturnal migrant passerines are more susceptible to collision (NRC 2007).  This is likely influenced by the relatively high abundance of passerines as well as their migration flight behaviors.  However, common species within this avian group are generally less susceptible to population-level impacts than other avian groups, such as raptors, due to their relatively high abundance.

Four species of bird were found as fatalities (not including unidentified passerine).  None of the avian species found are listed in the state of New York.  The majority of birds found were nocturnal migrant songbirds.  A single raptor was however found incidentally by First Wind staff. Passerines have represented the majority (72.4%) of avian species found at wind farms in the east and midwest while raptors have represented 5.3 percent of documented avian fatalities (Arnett 2005, Arnett _et al._ 2009, Derby _et al._ 2007, Drake _et al._ 2010, Fiedler _et al._ 2007, Gruver 2009, Howe 2002, Jain _et al_ . 2007, Jain _et al._ 2008, Jain _et al._ 2009a, Jain _et al._ 2009b, Jain _et al._ 2009c, Jain _et al._ 2009d, Johnson _et al._ 2000 and 2002, Kerns and Kerlinger 2004, Koford _et al._ 2005, Miller 2008, NJ Audubon Society 2009, Osborn _et al_ . 2000, Piorkowski 2006, Stantec 2008, Stantec 2009a, Stantec 2009b, Stantec 2009c, Stantec 2010a, Tidhar 2009, Vlietstra 2008, Young _et al._ 2009).  The 2010 composition and proportion of avian species groups found as fatalities at the Cohocton and Dutch Hill Wind Farm are consistent with these other studies. Bird fatalities peaked during the fall migration period; however, fatalities did occur in the spring and summer.  While the majority of passerine fatalities at wind farms in the U.S. have occurred during migration seasons, studies have documented fatalities during the breeding season (NRC 2007).

## **3.0 Acoustic Bat Survey**

## **3.1 INTRODUCTION**

Nine species of bats occur in New York, based upon their normal geographical range.  These are the little brown bat, northern long-eared bat, Indiana bat ( _Myotis sodalis_ ), eastern smallfooted bat ( _M. leibii_ ), silver-haired bat, tri-colored bat ( _Perimyotis subflavus_ ), big brown bat, eastern red bat, and hoary bat (Whitaker and Hamilton 1998).  Of these, the Indiana bat is listed as federally endangered, and the small-footed bat is a state-listed species of special concern.

Bats use high frequency echolocation to maneuver through the landscape during migration or in search of food and water.  Although echolocation sounds produced by bats fall above the range of human hearing, electronic recording equipment can be used to listen in on these high frequency calls.  Acoustic sampling of bat activity has become a standard tool of pre- and post construction surveys for wind-energy developments.  Acoustic sampling allows for simultaneous data collection at varying heights above ground level and across long time periods (Kunz _et al._ 2007).  These surveys can provide insight into altitudinal and seasonal patterns of bat activity. While this type of data collection cannot determine the number of individuals found in an area,

and is associated with several major assumptions (Hayes 2000), it can be used to examine activity trends for certain species or species groups.  For pre-construction surveys, these methods may be useful in predicting potential post-construction mortality patterns.  For postconstruction surveys, acoustic surveys can indicate bat use patterns which may be compared to turbine collision patterns.  A bat acoustic survey was conducted in 2010 during Year 2 operations at the Project.  The protocol for the 2010 study was developed by First Wind in cooperation with the NYSDEC and USFWS, and included a provision that bat acoustic sampling would be conducted from April 26 to October 22, 2010.

Currently, acoustic methods emphasize monitoring a vertical array of airspace to document species flying at all altitudes (Arnett _et al._ 2006, Kunz _et al_ . 2007, Reynolds 2006).  Bat fatalities occur when individuals collide with turbines (Horn _et al._ 2008) or come in close proximity to spinning blades, which can result in rapid decompression that leads to death as a result of barotrauma (Baerwald _et al_ . 2008).  Detectors placed at or near rotor-swept height likely record bats most at risk of collision or barotrauma from spinning turbine blades.  Acoustic surveys at the Project area were designed to monitor bat activity within the rotor swept zone as well habitats adjacent to turbines included in the mortality surveys in an attempt to correlate activity rates with mortality events.

## **3.2 METHODS**

## **3.2.1 Data Collection Methods**

Anabat SD1 detectors (Titley Electronics Pty Ltd.) were used for the duration of the 2010 acoustic bat survey.  Anabat detectors are frequency division detectors, dividing the frequency of echolocation sounds made by bats by a factor of 16, and recording these sounds for subsequent analysis.  The audio sensitivity setting of each Anabat system was set between six and seven (on a scale of one to ten) to maximize sensitivity while limiting ambient background noise which may cause interference.  The sensitivity of individual detectors was then tested using an ultrasonic Bat Chirp (Reno, NV) to ensure that the detectors would be able to detect bats up to a distance of approximately 30 m (98’).  Detectors were programmed to passively record data between 7:00 pm and 7:00 am via the internal clock on the SD1 detector, and data was stored on removable compact flash cards (1-2 GB).  Anabat detectors were selected based upon their widespread use for this type of survey, their ability to be deployed for long periods of time, and their ability to detect a broad frequency range, which allows detection of all species of bats that could occur in the Project area.

Each Anabat detector was powered by 12-volt batteries charged by solar panels.  Each solarpowered Anabat system was deployed in waterproof housing enabling the detector to record while unattended for the duration of the survey.  The housing suspends the Anabat microphone downward to give maximum protection from precipitation.  To compensate for the downward position, a curved plastic joint was used to funnel sound into the downward-facing microphone, allowing the microphone to record the airspace horizontally surrounding the detector.

## **3.2.2 Site Selection**

Detectors deployed above canopy height more readily survey long-distance migrants; these species generally fly and forage at high altitudes, and are species that experience the highest

turbine collision rates (Arnett _et al._ 2008).  Accordingly, one detector was deployed in the cable array of a 60 m met tower (at an elevation of approximately 40 m) on Pine Hill, located at a northeastern location within the Project.  The detector is suspended over a small wetland edge habitat along the border of two agricultural fields (Figures 3-1 and 3-2a).

**Figure 3-2a.** Met tower detector.

Tree level detectors are deployed because (1) resident bat species generally forage close to, or below, the tree canopy, (2) activity is often greater at ground level, so these detectors assist with species presence and activity patterns, and (3) bats present at ground level could potentially become attracted to the height of rotating blades (Cryan and Barclay 2009, Kunz _et al._ 2007). Two detectors were suspended from trees adjacent to turbine clearings; one at turbine 22 on Lent Hill and a second at turbine 2A on Dutch Hill (Figure 3-1).  The turbine 2A detector was suspended approximately 2.5 m high along the edge of a hardwood forest dominated by mature maple; the site is adjacent to an actively managed hayfield (Figure 3-2b). The microphone was aimed along the edge habitat of the hayfield and was placed near an opening between two fields.

**Figure 3-2b.** Turbine 2A detector.

The turbine 22 detector was deployed approximately 2 m high along a wooded edge next to a farm road overgrown with tall grasses and bramble (Figure 3-2c).  The surrounding forest at the site is a mix of beech regrowth and mature maple and white pine.

## **3.2.3 Data Analysis Methods**

Ultrasound recordings of bat echolocation may be broken into recordings of a single bat call or recordings of bat call sequences.  A call is a single pulse of sound produced by a bat, while a call sequence is a combination of two or more pulses recorded in an Anabat file.  Recordings containing less than two calls were eliminated from analysis as has been done in similar studies (Arnett _et al_ . 2006).

Potential call files were extracted from data files using CFCread[] software.  The default settings for CFCread[] were used during this file extraction process, as these settings are recommended for the calls that are characteristic of New York bats.  This software screens all data recorded by the bat detector and extracts call files using a filter.  Using the default settings for this initial screen also ensures comparability between data sets.  Settings used by the filter include a max TBC (time between calls) of 5 seconds, a minimum line length of 5 milliseconds, and a smoothing factor of 50.  The smoothing factor refers to whether or not adjacent pixels can be connected with a smooth line.  The higher the smoothing factor, the less restrictive the filter is and the more noise files and poor quality call sequences are retained within the data set.

Following extraction of call files, each file was visually inspected for species identification and to ensure that only bat calls were included in the data set.  Insect activity, wind, and interference sometimes produce Anabat files that pass through the initial filter and need to be visually inspected and removed from the data set.  Call sequences are easily differentiated from other recordings, which typically form a diffuse band of dots at either a constant frequency or widely varying frequency.

Because bat activity levels are highly variable among individual nights and individual hours (Hayes 1997, Arnett _et al_ . 2006), detection rates are summarized on both of these temporal scales.  Nightly detection rates were summarized by month as well as for the entire sampling period.  Hourly detection rates were summarized by hour after sunset, as recommended by Kunz _et al_ . (2007).  Quantitative comparisons among these temporal periods were not attempted because the high amount of variability associated with bat detection would require much larger sample sizes (Arnett _et al_ . 2006, Hayes 1997).

Bat call sequences were individually marked and categorized by species group or “guild” based on visual comparison to reference calls.  Qualitative visual comparison of recorded call sequences of sufficient length to reference libraries of bat calls allows for relatively accurate identification of bat species (O’Farrell _et al_ . 1999, O’Farrell and Gannon 1999).  Call sequences were classified to species whenever possible, based on criteria developed from review of reference calls collected by Chris Corben, the developer of the Anabat system, as well as other bat researchers.  However, due to similarity of call signatures between several species, all classified calls have been categorized into five guilds[4] reflecting the bat community in the region of the Project area and is as follows:

- **Unknown (UNKN)** – All call sequences with less than five calls, or poor quality sequences (those with indistinct call characteristics or background static).  These sequences were further identified as either “high frequency unknown” (HFUN) for sequences with a minimum frequency above 30 to 35 kHz, or “low frequency unknown” (LFUN) for sequences with a minimum frequency below 30 to 35 kHz.

- **Myotis (MYSP)** – All bats of the genus _Myotis_ .  While there are some general characteristics believed to be distinctive for several of the species in this genus, these characteristics do not occur consistently enough for any one species to be identified reliably at all times when using Anabat recordings.

- **Eastern red bat/tri-colored bat[5] (RBTB)** – Eastern red bats and tri-colored bats. These two species can produce calls most distinctive to each species.  However, significant overlap in the call pulse shape, frequency range, and slope can also occur.

- **Big brown/silver-haired bat (BBSH)** – Big brown and silver-haired bats.  These species’ call signatures commonly overlap and have therefore been included as one guild in this report.

- **Hoary bat (HB)** – Hoary bats.  Calls of hoary bats can usually be distinguished from those of big brown and silver-haired bats by minimum frequency extending below 20 kHz or by calls varying widely in minimum frequency across a sequence.

This method of guild identification represents a conservative approach to bat call identification. Since some species sometimes produce calls unique only to that species, all calls were identified to the lowest possible taxonomic level before being grouped into the listed guilds. Tables and figures in the body of this report will reflect those guilds.  However, since speciesspecific identification did occur in some cases, each guild will also be briefly discussed with respect to potential species composition of recorded call sequences.

Once all of the call files were identified and categorized in appropriate guilds, nightly tallies of detected calls were compiled.  Mean detection rates (number of recordings/detector-night) for the entire sampling period were calculated for each detector and for all detectors combined.

## **3.2.3.1 Weather Data**

Temperature (°C) and wind speed (m/s) were recorded at 10-minute intervals by the Pine Hill met tower.  Wind speed data and temperature data were collected from sensors located at hub height on a turbine nacelle.  The mean, maximum, and minimum temperature and wind speed were calculated for each night.
